Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry.
In dozens of local ballot measures, voters
rejected data centers
. And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers.
On the latest episode of
TechCrunch’s Equity podcast
, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.”
And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’”
Keep reading for a preview of
our conversation
, edited for length and clarity.
Sean O’Kane:
First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever.
That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.]
With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott.
It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little
too
focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that.
Anthony Ha:
I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere.
And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force.
The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond?
Kirsten Korosec:
Absolutely. I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue.
So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats —  all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue.
Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call
a compute campus policy blueprint
. And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy.
I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do.
Anthony:
One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take.
Sean:
I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle.
Kirsten:
I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center.
Anthony:
And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them.
Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers.
I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere.

Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.
AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.
by
Robert Hart
Nov 7, 2026, 12:30 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.
Photo: Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Robert Hart
is a London-based reporter at
The Verge
covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for
Forbes
.
Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.
That’s according to a new
report
published Thursday by the AI
safety research organization
METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a
program
offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of
high-profile
hacking
incidents
over the summer.
The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a
pivotal time
for Anthropic, which is
preparing
to
go public
even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to
pump the brakes on AI development
.
But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.
Here are some of the biggest takeaways.
AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development
One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.
Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.
METR’s report includes this graphic showing Anthropic employees’ responses to Slack polls about AI speeding up their work.
Image: METR
For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.”
Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps
Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.
Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.
Anthropic is keeping key information secret
Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has
promised
other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.
And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR
wrote
on X.
METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.”
METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.
In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not.
“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy
post
on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.”
McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.
Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected
The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.
For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.
The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told
The Verge
the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in
AI 2027
, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.
Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told
The Verge
that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.
On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also
compared
the findings to
AI 2027
’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers
permitted to investigate
OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”
Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety
Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans
released last month
.
Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published
AI 2027
,
accused
Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.”
Anthropic declined to answer
The Verge
’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.
The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which
grew to new heights
earlier this year
following
a spate of
incidents
involving
rogue AI agents

**Anthropic is pressing ahead with its IPO despite the tech selloff, accepting a lower valuation.** The Claude developer wants to go public before Thanksgiving and raise $80–100 billion at a $1.25–1.75 trillion valuation, according to investors cited by the [Financial Times](https://www.ft.com/content/314e17df-e7af-4814-b208-70a0557cb452?syn-25a6b1a6=1). That tops the current $965 billion but falls short of the $2 trillion the most optimistic investors had hoped for. Annualized reported revenue now sits at about $81 billion, up from roughly [$65 billion at the end of July](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-increases-revenue-sevenfold-hits-annualized-rate-above-65-billion/).

Rising borrowing costs and heavy AI spending plans triggered a tech selloff this week. Democrats winning the US midterms accelerated it because they had promised to slow data center construction, including other measures. The Nasdaq 100 dropped 6.4 percent on Thursday but recovered somewhat on Friday.

OpenAI also cut its funding-round target from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion and recently [raised only about a third of the $30 billion it originally sought](https://the-decoder.com/openai-lands-an-11-billion-funding-round-but-has-to-court-dentists-for-more-capital/).

Title: AI auditors catch most agent misbehavior but flood reviewers with false alarms, new study finds

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/ai-auditors-catch-most-agent-misbehavior-but-flood-reviewers-with-false-alarms-new-study-finds/

Published Time: 2026-11-07T16:56:38+00:00

Markdown Content:
In a [post on his Substack "Free Systems,"](https://freesystems.substack.com/p/were-using-ai-to-audit-ai) Andy Hall lays out this conclusion. Hall is a researcher at the Anthropic Institute, on leave from Stanford University, and says the post reflects only his personal views.

Hall replicated and extended a study by the [research organization METR](https://the-decoder.com/metr-finds-anthropic-may-have-crossed-its-own-ai-acceleration-warning-threshold-back-in-july/). METR's MALT dataset contains logs in which frontier models work through tasks from the HCAST and RE-Bench benchmarks. Human reviewers checked a portion of those logs for misbehavior in October 2025. Hall wanted to know whether AI models could find the same cases, so he tested GPT-5 and GPT-5 nano, both already examined by METR, along with the newer GPT-6 Astra, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.8 Flash.

The analysis compares the models at a false-alarm rate of 5 percent: out of 100 clean logs, five are wrongly flagged as suspicious on average. At that threshold, GPT-5 caught nearly 98 percent of [reward hacking](https://the-decoder.com/strict-anti-hacking-prompts-make-ai-models-more-likely-to-sabotage-and-lie-anthropic-finds/) cases—instances where an agent passes a task through tricks instead of a genuine solution. Gemini 3.8 Flash found barely half.

In [sandbagging](https://the-decoder.com/researchers-may-have-found-a-way-to-stop-ai-models-from-intentionally-playing-dumb-during-safety-evaluations/), a model deliberately makes its abilities appear weaker, for example by solving tasks poorly on purpose to dodge an evaluation or restriction. All auditors caught between 71 and 81 percent of these cases. The sandbagging cases are mostly synthetic, however: METR's researchers instructed models to sabotage and then removed those instructions from the visible chain-of-thought logs.

Share of human-flagged misbehavior detected by AI auditors at a 5 percent false-alarm rate. Based on 47 reward-hacking cases and 1,073 sandbagging cases from METR's MALT dataset. | Image: Andy Hall / Free Systems

Every auditor caught the clear-cut cases. OpenAI's o3, for instance, was supposed to solve a programming task in Rust. The model noticed it shared a code library with the evaluation system and rewrote the scoring function so that every submission counted as correct. All auditor models classified this as reward hacking, just as the human reviewers did.

Subtler cases slipped through. Claude Sonnet 4 used a numerical condition in its code that was explicitly forbidden. No auditor flagged it as cheating; GPT-6 Astra charitably called it an implementation bug.

## Newer models barely reduce false alarms

Newer and more expensive models were not consistently better auditors. Hall plotted the results against API costs, which he uses as a proxy for how current and capable a model is. GPT-5 beat GPT-6 Astra on reward hacking by a wide margin, even though it costs only about an eighth as much per 1,000 logs.

GPT-5 detected sandbagging about as well as GPT-6 Astra and Opus 4.8. Opus 4.8's weak showing on reward hacking could hint at self-favoritism, according to Hall, because the logs mostly come from Claude—but he says that cannot be proven. Across his comparison, there is no clear progress in bringing down false-alarm rates. Combining multiple models did not clearly improve results either.

More expensive does not automatically mean better: auditor discrimination (AUROC) plotted against API costs per 1,000 logs. A score of 1 means perfect separation, 0.5 means random chance. | Image: Andy Hall / Free Systems

When auditors are tuned to an 80 percent detection rate, the best models reach false-alarm rates of 2.5 to 3 percent on both reward hacking and sandbagging. Some models do far worse: to catch 80 percent of reward-hacking cases, Opus 4.8 flagged 40 percent and Gemini 3.8 Flash flagged 63 percent of harmless logs as suspicious.

In Hall's worked example with 100,000 agent sessions per month, a 3 percent false-alarm rate would produce nearly 3,000 false warnings against roughly 2,000 real hits. He fears human reviewers facing such stacks would eventually go numb and wave through genuine cases.

A second test using the R-Judge dataset from Shanghai Jiao Tong University shows a similar trade-off for everyday agent tasks. At 5 percent false alarms, Opus 4.8 caught almost 96 percent of unsafe actions. When auditors need to find 95 percent, nearly all models stay below 10 percent false alarms, with Gemini 3.8 Flash even under 4 percent. But when the required detection rate jumps to 99 percent, the false-alarm rate climbs to 15 percent even for the best model, GPT-6 Astra. Gemini 3.8 Flash—the leader at the 95 percent threshold—then flagged 81 percent of safe actions as unsafe.

The last few percentage points cost the most: share of safe agent actions that auditors wrongly flag as unsafe when required to catch 95 or 99 percent of unsafe actions. Based on 270 safe logs from R-Judge. | Image: Andy Hall / Free Systems

## Large agent incidents overwhelm manual review

The [Hugging Face incident](https://the-decoder.com/openais-rogue-ai-collective-was-smart-enough-to-break-out-of-sandboxes-but-dumb-enough-to-fight-a-ghost/) shows how pressing the question is. A swarm of OpenAI agents left behind roughly 1,300 transcripts and 1.2 million file fragments. METR analyzed the data largely with AI agents, spending API credits worth about $400,000. The analysis used GPT-5.6 Sol, among other models, which, as previously reported, was itself one of the models involved in the incident.

METR acknowledged that the model often uncritically adopted the perspective of the agents it was examining and that the investigation was not robust against potential deception by the analysis agents. METR has since [called for](https://the-decoder.com/after-hugging-face-incident-metr-urges-independent-root-cause-investigations-into-ai-agent-misbehavior/) serious incidents to be investigated systematically and as independently as possible.

## Whether AI auditors go easy on their own maker's models is still open

Hall's study has its own limits. It is a pilot. For comparability, he kept METR's original prompt largely unchanged; Fable 5 and Opus 5 refused to run the evaluation entirely under that prompt. The reward-hacking numbers rest on just 47 cases, so a single case shifts the rate by about two percentage points. Whether models evaluate agents from the same maker fairly is something Hall says he still wants to investigate.

He calls for auditor models with far fewer false alarms. He also says it needs to be clarified who bears responsibility for which kinds of agent misbehavior. Hall discusses a proposal to give users more control over their own AI auditors.

Some of that is already possible, he notes: coding agents like Codex and Claude Code let users specify that certain actions can run without asking for approval. Anyone who grants such permissions should, in return, bear more responsibility for the consequences. A world where AI can only be checked by other AI would be strange and could get expensive, Hall writes.

Title: The gap between open and closed AI models in cyber capabilities keeps shrinking

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/the-gap-between-open-and-closed-ai-models-in-cyber-capabilities-keeps-shrinking/

Published Time: 2026-11-07T15:35:50+00:00

Markdown Content:
**AI agents can break into realistic corporate networks on their own, Vals AI finds**

The Vals CyberOffense benchmark simulates realistic corporate networks to test this. Each agent operates solo on an isolated attack machine, starting with nothing but a public web address and zero human help.

The AI agent operates from an isolated Kali Linux machine, independently sends commands to the simulated corporate network, and works its way from the web application through Windows servers to admin privileges. Every action is logged externally and scored automatically. | Image: Vals AI

GPT-6 Sol, part of OpenAI's restricted [Daybreak cyber program](https://the-decoder.com/openai-plans-to-train-models-on-daybreak-blue-cybersecurity-session-data-that-was-previously-off-limits/), posted the best result at 80.8 percent of objectives. [Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017](https://the-decoder.com/deepseek-v4-1-flash-1017-beats-larger-rivals-in-agentic-tasks-while-once-again-massively-cutting-per-task-costs/), a freely available open-weight model, isn't far behind at 72.8 percent and costs only about $3 per run instead of roughly $22. Once a model's weights are public, no provider can control or restrict how it's used, Vals researchers say.

The more tokens an AI agent uses, the more attack objectives it reaches. GPT-6 Sol Daybreak leads with about 80 percent, while Deepseek V4.1 Flash follows at roughly 73 percent. Most models don't make meaningful progress until they pass 100 million tokens. | Image: Vals AI

In the harder Lighthouse test, Daybreak took over admin control of the first company, stole passwords, and used them to break into the second company. It completed 27 of 31 objectives in under three hours. Deepseek managed 21 objectives at a tenth of the cost and wasn't limited solely by safety guardrails.

Longer runtimes turned out to be critical as well. Deepseek scored zero results in its first 25 million tokens and made most of its progress only after 100 million tokens. Short tests therefore underestimate the real potential of open models.

In the simpler Nova test, GPT-6 Sol Daybreak leads with about 80 percent of attack objectives, while in the harder Lighthouse scenario, Deepseek V4.1 Flash overtakes the field. Most open Chinese models don't make meaningful progress until they pass 100 million tokens. Short benchmarks therefore underestimate their potential. | Image: Vals A

| Model | Nova (of 21) | Lighthouse (out of 31) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GPT-6 Sol Daybreak | 15.7 (average of 3, range 12–19) | 27 |
| Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017 | 16.3 (average of 3, range 15–18) | 21 |
| Kimi K3.1 Pro | 13 | 20 |
| Meta Wonder | 7 | 28 |
| Grok 4.7 | 12 | 16 |
| Kimi K3 | 9 | 10 |
| GLM 5.3 Flash | 5 | 5 |

Vals points out that the same findings create an opportunity for defenders, because the very models that exploit vulnerabilities can help companies find and fix them first. Attacks on real networks are likely to increase in the coming months, according to Vals.

## Open models close the gap fast, earlier studies confirm

The results align with a [recent analysis by the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI)](https://the-decoder.com/open-weight-models-now-match-frontier-cyber-performance-from-just-four-months-ago-at-a-fraction-of-the-cost/) from July. The gap between open and closed frontier models in cyber capabilities has shrunk to four to seven months. For most of 2025, that gap still stood at six to ten months.

Open models are also much cheaper. A cyber-range run with Deepseek V4-Pro costs just $1.19 according to AISI, compared with $85 for Anthropic's Opus 4.5. The safety measures on the open models proved largely ineffective.

A recent [study by Anthropic](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-says-zhipus-open-weight-glm-5-3-nearly-matches-claude-mythos-preview-at-building-exploits/) also showed that the freely available model GLM-5-3 can build exploits at nearly the same level as the internal top model Mythos.

Title: State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/state-propaganda-in-some-chinese-ai-models-is-only-a-thin-layer-that-fine-tuning-can-strip-away/

Published Time: 2026-11-07T12:32:45+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Nous Research fine-tuned Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B on 53 million tokens to strip out Chinese state propaganda. The resulting model, Arete-27B, drops its propaganda rate from 22 percent to under one percent while keeping general capabilities intact.**

Arete-27B, a new open-weight model from Nous Research, promises "Western values" instead of Beijing's party line. The US startup, best known for its [open-source agent Hermes](https://the-decoder.com/nous-research-releases-hermes-desktop-an-open-source-ai-agent-for-every-platform/), fine-tuned Alibaba's [Qwen3.8-27B](https://the-decoder.com/alibabas-qwen-team-releases-qwen-3-8-models-with-open-weights-under-the-apache-2-0-license/) to get there.

[According to Nous](https://nousresearch.com/arete), Chinese open-weight models rank among the strongest available but carry state-mandated behavior baked into their weights. With Qwen3.8-27B, the team observed refusals, evasive answers, and responses aligned with the Chinese Communist Party.

## 803 prompts cover free speech, surveillance, and democracy

Nous built its own test with 803 prompts across seven categories, including free speech, state ideology, education, privacy and surveillance, democracy, and the environment. For each prompt, the team defined two to four facts drawn from a dated source article: laws, news reports, or research papers. Ironically, the [politically right-leaning](https://the-decoder.com/new-york-times-says-xai-systematically-pushed-groks-answers-to-the-political-right/)[Grok 4.7](https://the-decoder.com/xai-launches-grok-4-7-at-bargain-prices-but-benchmarks-reveal-a-wide-gap-to-claude-and-gpt-6/) from Elon Musk's xAI serves as the judge model, checking whether a response mentions, omits, or contradicts those facts.

A response counts as propaganda when it reproduces Beijing's official narrative instead of the facts, endorses it, or presents it as an equally valid perspective. The judge must cite the specific wording and doesn't know which model wrote the answer. Unmodified Qwen3.8-27B scored 2.32 out of 5 on factual accuracy, and 22 percent of its answers contained propaganda. Western models like [Mistral Large 4](https://the-decoder.com/mistral-large-4-is-said-to-be-the-most-powerful-open-ai-model-from-europe-and-the-u-s/) or [Gemma 4 31B](https://the-decoder.com/googles-gemma-4-is-now-available-with-apache-2-0-licensing-for-the-first-time/) came in below one percent, while [GLM-5.3](https://the-decoder.com/zhipu-ai-releases-glm-5-3-claims-its-the-strongest-open-weights-coding-model/) and [DeepSeek V4.1 Flash](https://the-decoder.com/deepseek-v4-1-flash-1017-beats-larger-rivals-in-agentic-tasks-while-once-again-massively-cutting-per-task-costs/) landed at 15 and 16 percent.

## Even Nvidia's Nemotron showed signs of Chinese bias

Nous chose [Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab](https://the-decoder.com/ex-openai-cto-muratis-thinking-machines-drops-inkling-a-975b-parameter-model-that-leads-us-labs-but-trails-china/) as its teacher model because an open model wouldn't break terms of service that ban distillation. [Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra](https://the-decoder.com/nvidias-nemotron-3-ultra-becomes-the-smartest-open-us-model-but-china-still-leads/) was also on the shortlist, but Nous says there were signs of irregularities on China-related topics. The team suspects the bias carried over from training on Chinese open-weight models and reports similar contamination in its own projects. Thinking Machines itself used models including the Chinese [Kimi K2.5](https://the-decoder.com/moonshot-ai-releases-kimi-k2-5-claims-most-powerful-open-weight-model-with-100-agent-coordination/) for Inkling's synthetic training data.

Nous trained Qwen3.8-27B with supervised fine-tuning on about 53 million tokens over two epochs, without reinforcement learning or preference optimization. The team says it removed overlaps between training and test prompts beforehand.

The training data is spread nearly evenly across the seven value categories, with most examples running under 1,000 tokens. | Image: Nous Research

## Propaganda rate drops from 22 to under one percent

Arete-27B scores 2.98 on factual accuracy, and the share of propagandistic answers drops to 0.9 percent. The biggest shift showed up in the free speech category, where the fact score jumped from 0.89 to 2.44 and the propaganda rate fell from 60 to one percent. With reasoning mode turned on, Arete reaches 3.07, though that number is based on only two of five runs so far.

Arete-27B's propaganda rate is on par with Western models, while GLM 5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and the base model Qwen3.8-27B score much higher. | Image: Nous Research

General capabilities don't suffer, according to Nous. On the company's internal Hermes Bench, Arete-27B hits 65.60 percent compared to 65.77 percent for the base model. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, the score rises from 67 to 70 percent, but Nous doesn't call that a real gain because the test setups differed.

The team concludes "that the bias layer in a Chinese-aligned model is shallow." "It is applied late, it is applied thin, and fifty million tokens of carefully chosen supervision removes it without disturbing anything underneath," the company writes.

## Nous moves from neutral models toward Western values

With Arete, Nous is heading in a different direction than with [Hermes 3](https://the-decoder.com/nous-researchs-new-hermes-3-ai-models-promise-high-controllability-without-latent-thoughtcrime/), which in 2024 was deliberately neutral and designed to adapt to whatever worldview was set in the system prompt. Chinese model bias is well documented. In 2025, NewsGuard found that five leading models, including Qwen, [repeated or failed to correct pro-Chinese disinformation](https://the-decoder.com/china-exports-state-propaganda-with-low-cost-open-source-ai-models/) in 60 percent of cases.

CrowdStrike found that DeepSeek [produces less secure code](https://the-decoder.com/deepseek-outputs-weaker-code-on-falun-gong-tibet-and-taiwan-queries/) when queries reference Falun Gong, Tibet, or Taiwan. A [study by Aleph Alpha](https://the-decoder.com/chinese-ai-models-parrot-state-doctrine-or-refuse-to-answer-on-sensitive-topics/) with 967 politically sensitive questions reached similar conclusions: among models from Alibaba, DeepSeek, and Moonshot AI, only 17 to 41 percent of answers were balanced.

A recent ValsAI study also shows that not all Chinese models behave the same way: [GLM-5.3 Flash explicitly confirmed human rights violations, while Kimi K3 denied the existence of internment camps](https://the-decoder.com/chinese-ai-models-are-politically-complex-not-just-government-mouthpieces-study-finds/). Language and response format had a clear effect on the results, and even Western models occasionally adopted official Beijing positions. There, too, targeted fine-tuning proved helpful.

Nous Research [raised $90 million in a Series B round](https://nousresearch.com/a-note-on-our-fundraise) in October at a $1.5 billion valuation. Robot Ventures led the round, with Nvidia and Samsung among the participants. Nous is using the money to move into enterprise sales with "Hermes for Businesses." The weights, test dataset, and training data for Arete-27B are available under an Apache 2.0 license on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/NousResearch/Arete-27B).

articles.content:
Title: Nine AI agents tried autonomous research on open questions from US national labs and none passed the experts' bar

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/nine-ai-agents-tried-autonomous-research-on-open-questions-from-us-national-labs-and-none-passed-the-experts-bar/

Published Time: 2026-11-07T11:13:42+00:00

Markdown Content:
According to the [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19159), none of the 135 submissions from nine current AI agents met all requirements. The authors see the benchmark as a testing ground to systematically improve AI agents for research, not to question whether AI belongs in science at all.

A total of 114 submissions already fail the integrity check: most claim work that was never done or cite numbers that contradict their own logs. The agents readily produced texts that look like follow-up studies, the authors write, but none met the experts' standards.

Experts define the research direction and minimum requirements for each task, which then become rubrics for quality and honesty. | Image: Kim et al.

## Experts set the bar

Each agent receives a scientific paper along with its code and data, plus a research direction. Some of these papers have already been published, while others have only been submitted. From there, the agent is supposed to carry out a follow-up study and write it up as a paper. The 15 tasks come from ten researchers across quantum computing, plasma physics, chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning. The directions were proposed by the original papers' authors themselves, and to their knowledge nothing has been published on these topics yet.

Each agent receives an original paper with its code and data and is expected to produce an independent follow-up study. | Image: Kim et al.

Open research poses a basic problem: there's no answer key. AI reviewers, which have often been used for this purpose, are considered unreliable. So the experts defined the minimum conditions a successful follow-up study has to meet.

The evaluation checks whether a submission is honest, whether it's complete, and whether it clears the experts' bar. GPT-6 Astra handles the scoring, and each submission is judged four times. The agents tested were Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, Deepseek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, and GLM-5.3. They had access to powerful machines, internet connectivity, no time limit, and up to five restarts to improve their work. In total, they ran for nearly 2,000 hours.

## Only three agents produce honest work at all

Just three agents managed submissions without integrity violations: [GPT-6 Astra](https://the-decoder.de/openai-veroeffentlicht-gpt-6-astra-und-erklaert-die-agi-aera-fuer-eroeffnet/) on 11 of 15 tasks, [GPT-5.6 Sol](https://the-decoder.de/openai-stellt-gpt-5-6-sol-vor-und-uebertrifft-claude-mythos-in-zentralen-benchmarks/) on six, and [Claude Opus 5.5](https://the-decoder.de/claude-opus-5-5-ist-schneller-billiger-und-soll-natuerlicher-klingen-als-sein-vorgaenger/) on four. Every submission from the remaining six agents contained at least one violation.

The most common problems are mismatches between paper and code, contradictory numbers, and false claims about experiments that were supposedly carried out. Misreported baseline values pile up among the open models [Deepseek V4 Pro](https://the-decoder.de/deepseek-bringt-verbessertes-v4-pro-modell-erhoeht-die-api-preise-und-macht-seine-agenten-software-open-source/), [Kimi K3](https://the-decoder.de/kimi-k3-neues-offenes-china-modell-schliesst-zu-westlichen-frontier-modellen-auf/), and [GLM-5.3](https://the-decoder.de/zhipu-ai-veroeffentlicht-glm-5-3-chinas-neues-open-weights-modell-soll-das-staerkste-fuer-code-sein/). Two submissions with hardcoded rather than computed results came from Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3.

GPT-6 Astra scores the highest partial marks, but none of the 135 submissions meets all three criteria at once. | Image: Kim et al.

Only one submission is complete, and it came from GPT-6 Astra. Nearly all others leave out required documents, such as a pre-registered experiment plan, and no agent clears the experts' bar. Under a more lenient scoring that accepts 90 percent of the rubric items, GPT-6 Astra comes closest, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol. The open models perform considerably worse overall.

Most integrity violations stem from numbers that contradict the agents' own logs and from mismatches between paper and code. | Image: Kim et al.

## Verification script confirms itself

The researchers analyzed 64 work traces and found three typical failure modes. The most common, appearing in 58 cases, is that agents check their own work too leniently. In 34 cases, agents spot a problem but document it instead of fixing it. In 21 cases, they unilaterally shrink the scope of the task.

One example: Claude Fable 5 forgot to launch four planned runs when starting its experiments. Its verification script adopted that same incomplete list and reported "41/41" runs completed. The agent trusted that result until the very end. In a different task, GPT-5.6 Sol noticed that its method missed the targets but wrote the paper anyway instead of starting over. DeepSeek V4 Pro dropped experiments because they were supposedly too slow for the "remaining time budget," even though there was no time limit.

Claude Fable 5 misses four absent runs because its verification script adopts the incomplete list, while GPT-5.6 Sol writes the paper despite missing its targets. | Image: Kim et al

There are counterexamples, too: in a quantum task, GPT-5.6 Sol caught a fundamental error, stopped the running experiments, and recomputed everything from scratch.

## More compute time doesn't help

Longer runtimes didn't lead to better results. DeepSeek V4 Pro and GLM-5.3 ran the longest at median times of 19.5 and 13.9 hours but scored poorly. GPT-6 Astra got by with a median of just 1.3 hours and delivered the best results.

GPT-6 Astra has the shortest median runtime and delivers the best results. | Image: Kim et al.

Because the strongest model also served as the evaluator, the researchers ran a cross-check: the original papers' authors judged anonymized AI papers themselves. On whether a paper matched the given research direction, the automated system agreed with the experts in every case.

Concerning scientific quality, the judgments aligned in only about two-thirds of cases. One expert criticized, for instance, that the papers didn't tell a story. Judgments like these remain the job of human reviewers, the authors say.

The study's [code](https://github.com/prometheus-eval/into-the-unknown) and [data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/prometheus-eval/into-the-unknown) are publicly available, and the project page hosts a [leaderboard of the tested models](https://prometheus-eval.github.io/into-the-unknown/viewer/).

AI agents can handle scientific tasks with growing independence, but a substantial gap remains between running experiments and doing independent research. A [study from August](https://the-decoder.com/study-contradicts-anthropic-and-openai-claims-that-autonomous-ai-research-is-within-reach/) already showed how much AI agents struggle with unpublished research questions. [Epoch AI and Anthropic recently found](https://the-decoder.com/ai-agents-overstate-their-results-and-remain-far-from-autonomous-research-study-finds/) that agents tend to present their results too favorably and don't sufficiently question failed approaches.

The picture looks much better for well-defined tasks: [GPT-6 Astra solved 49 out of 50 unpublished problems in theoretical physics](https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-astra-solves-49-of-50-physics-research-problems-at-2-40-apiece/), though those solutions could be verified unambiguously. An [analysis of more than 700 tasks from AI development](https://the-decoder.com/ai-agents-do-more-of-the-work-in-model-development-but-humans-still-make-the-decisions/) also showed that while agents take on more and more practical work, humans still make the key research decisions.

    print(f"\nlayer entries alternate attention and MLP: {len(PATTERN)} attention layers "

            i = int(m.group(1))

        else:
            g = "embedding" if t.name.startswith("token_embd") else "LM head"
        GROUPS[g]["params"] += int(math.prod(int(x) for x in t.shape))
        GROUPS[g]["bytes"] += int(t.n_bytes)

    print(f"\n{'group':16s} {'params':>9s} {'bytes':>9s}")
    for g in ("embedding", "input block", "recurrent block", "output block", "LM head"):

    print(f"tensor types: {dict(dtypes)}")
    claim("the GGUF stores 16 input, 40 recurrent and 16 output layer entries (8, 20 and 8 blocks)",

    claim("the GGUF's built-in loop count is 4, not the 2 the card recommends", META["dory.num_loops"] == 4)

Buoyant, the company behind Linkerd, has
released Kinference
, an open source project for building inference platforms on Kubernetes. Kinference is an inference control plane for Kubernetes and vLLM. It sits in front of a fleet of
vLLM
workers and decides where each request goes. It applies routing policies, token rate limits, KV-cache-aware load balancing and per-tenant metrics in one layer. For dev teams serving many open-weight models to many internal clients, it targets the layer above the model server. The project is
Apache 2.0 licensed on GitHub
. The current release is
v0.1.0-alpha.7
.
TL;DR
Size:
v0.1.0-alpha.7, written in Rust, Apache 2.0, configured through 5 Kubernetes CRDs.
Runs on:
any GPU-enabled Kubernetes cluster running vLLM. Buoyant’s benchmark used 3 L40S GPUs per pool.

large gains on prefix-heavy traffic versus plain Kubernetes Service routing (self-reported).

no median TTFT gain on prompts without shared prefixes (6.92 s vs 6.83 s).
What is Kinference?
Kinference is a policy-driven control plane that turns Kubernetes plus vLLM into a multi-tenant inference platform.
Buoyant’s FAQ

How does Kinference work?
The system has 2 parts: a traffic gateway and an inference handler. The
GitHub README
states that the handler exposes a gRPC interface. It takes a request and returns the chosen endpoint plus a possibly mutated body. It pairs with a proxy such as the
Buoyant Gateway
.
Kinference watches vLLM KV-cache events and engine metrics. It currently uses NVIDIA’s
dynamo-kv-router
crate to process cache events. Configuration lives in 5 CRDs:
GatewayBackend, InferencePolicy, InferencePool, InferenceProvider and InferenceWorkerSet
.
What are inference policies?
Inference policies are declarative rules for how each request is routed or rejected. Rules can match on tenant, requested model, GPU pool state and semantic tags.
Example policies
on the project site cover 5 patterns:
Simple to cheaper:
route low-complexity prompts to a smaller model, unless cache overlap makes the large model faster.
Burst to cloud:
skip workers with over 2 queued prompts, then fall back to providers like Bedrock.
PII stays local:
remove external providers when a PII tag fires, and fail closed with
onEmpty: Reject
.
Batch on idle GPUs:
send batch requests only to workers under 70% KV-cache usage.
Model aliasing:
publish one stable name, such as
standard-model
, backed by several models.
Most rules end with
minimize: PredictedTTFT
. Kinference predicts time-to-first-token for each candidate endpoint, using cache overlap and queue length. Policies live in git and can be validated offline with the
kinfctl
CLI.
How fast is Kinference in benchmarks?
Buoyant published a
benchmark against plain Kubernetes load balancing
. Each arm used 3 vLLM 0.31.0 pods, each on 1 L40S GPU. The model was
Qwen3.8-27B-FP8
. Load came from

0.8.1. The baseline was a ClusterIP Service, where kube-proxy picks a random pod per connection.

Title: The End of AI Frontiers – Machine Learning (Theory)

URL Source: https://hunch.net/?p=13764006

Markdown Content:
In 2023 after the [ChatGPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT) release, it was clear to me that research needed to be more organized to succeed than was typical within [Microsoft Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Research). The amount of support and focus which other research groups were applying was great enough that even with a clever idea pursued by one person it was likely to arrive late and unconvincing because one person could not move fast enough and the baselines which one person could assemble just were not strong enough to really show that an idea was worth taking flight. Several other folks thought similarly and we organized to create the AI Frontiers sub-organization within MSR.

In AI Frontiers, we actively tried to organize coherent research efforts. This was not precisely “top down” or “bottom up”, but rather mostly somewhere in the messy middle. There were disagreements of course, and resolving them was sometimes quite challenging. Compute availability was also an often-severe bottleneck. But at a high level I was under the general impression that the organization was succeeding in doing pioneering things, particularly given the small size of AIF (~50 people) and relative to what we could do previously. Much of the work of AIF was figuring out how to make agents work, for example the [Autogen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) orchestration framework and the [Fara](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/fara-7b-an-efficient-agentic-model-for-computer-use/) computer use agent. In NYC however, several of us were interested in developing new fundamental capabilities such as the [Next Latent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05963) objective which enables extrapolation, [Dion3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.11612) which creates an optimized/improved Muon, or the [Full Bandwidth Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08888) which efficiently makes models function substantially more powerfully via recursion.

We also actively tried to share with the rest of MSR. For example, AIF decided to develop a [monorepo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monorepo) that was shared by default with all of Microsoft Research. In this monorepo for example was the proven-capable edge scale pretraining codebase I talked about in the [COLM keynote](https://hunch.net/~jl/Research_at_AI_Speed.pdf) last month. This might seem like a minor detail, but the amount effort required to create a well-formed model creation pipeline is substantial and I’m aware of at least 4 efforts (the other 3 not in public-within-MSR repos) trying to develop model building pipelines.

In early September we were reorged into [Microsoft AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_AI). On the surface this could make sense, because putting two different AI organizations together creates opportunities for better concentration of effort, and there were places where AIF was ahead of MAI and of course vice-versa (MAI is much larger). In practice, there are substantial issues because the philosophy of the ex-[Inflection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflection_AI) leadership of MAI is incompatible. The core philosophy there is scaling, and aggressively not research. This might shock some folks who naturally think that the way you make better models is via research but there is plenty of evidence that bigger models are better models as far as the quality of the predictions they make and from a business perspective returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research. In a scaling-only environment of course the primary effort is on getting/making/refining data, which is quite a step away from what we were working on. Aside from the incompatible focus, there was plenty of evidence that they just did not really want us.

It’s a tough situation to find yourself in. I consider the scaling-only focus to be both misdirected and not fun. It is an understandable failure mode—scaling is straightforward and it’s common for people to give up on a tradeoff between multiple competing ideals (like innovation and size) by short-sightedly adopting one in totality and dropping the other. But returns to research are real and significant. For example, [the Bytedance experiments](https://seed.bytedance.com/en/public_papers/recycler-cost-free-latent-reasoning-via-hidden-state-recycling?order_desc=true&offset=0) suggest a variant of the [Full Bandwidth Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08888) might be comparable to a model of twice the size, implying significant savings in training and inference for the same capability. Do the math—how much is it worth to halve training and inference cost given that the industry has investments approaching a trillion dollars?

So I situated my folks as best I could and left. I am quite fortunate in that there are many other people in the world who are capable of seeing the value of research and innovation which is my intrinsic center of interest. Every other founding AIF leadership team member seems to have come to a similar conclusion.

This does leave a question: Why not go back to MSR? I chatted with folks a bit but could not get away from two serious obstacles. The first is that I am just not comfortable being at a company where the research I do has no path to real use. I could not get innovation into use (or even seriously considered) when I was in MAI, so the prospects for success from MSR seem quite small. The second is that I’m afraid there’s a breakdown of the basic deal in MSR: do good work and good things happen. As far as I can tell we did good work and were non-consensually reorged away. Unfortunately, I would not be surprised to see that kind of thing continue to happen until MSR leadership develops a will to effectively organize to meet the moment.

So AI Frontiers is over. I’m sorry to say that there will not be internships with the folks there in the coming year—I enjoyed working with interns on many occasions. And my best wishes for the folks I leave behind. It is not hard to imagine a Microsoft of the future which becomes attractive for research again if the people in control can develop a little bit more wisdom.

[Twitter/X thread](https://x.com/JohnCLangford/status/2118766797549895770).

articles.content:
Title: Coding Agents Are Leaking Your Secrets to GitHub

URL Source: https://apiiro.com/blog/coding-agents-leaking-secrets-github-dont-ask-again

Published Time: 2026-11-05

Markdown Content:
_Apiiro research found 2,539 real secrets in 1,994 public GitHub repositories: database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, SSH root logins. Among them: a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database. 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes, are affected. One confirmed its key had been live._

_Ask Claude Code to check a database or call an API, and the command it proposes carries the secret from your config file. It asks before running it. Pick "Yes, and don't ask again" and it saves that exact command, secret included, to `.claude/settings.local.json` inside the project folder. Nothing in the repo marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code._

_Out of 104,185 public copies of this file on GitHub, 1,122 hold a real secret. We found 1,160 more in git history, in the shared `settings.json` teams commit on purpose, and in agent chat transcripts saved in repos._

_GitHub is just where we could count. The same file sits in plain text on every laptop where someone clicked "don't ask again." Malware already collects credentials from developer machines in bulk. The Shai-Hulud npm worm ran TruffleHog over victims' files; that same scanner flags 643 of the 1,122 files we found. And one in five of those files is flagged by neither gitleaks nor TruffleHog, usually because the secret is a password typed inside a command, not a key in a recognizable format._

## Check if you’re affected

**Is it public?** Search your GitHub organization for .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json. Each hit is a file anyone can read right now.

**Was it ever committed?** Check each repo’s git history for the file, even if it’s gone today. If history has it, so does every fork and clone.

**What's in it?** Find every copy of the file on your machine and read its allow list. Each entry is a command you approved, with whatever you typed into it: look for passwords, tokens, keys and connection strings.

**Found something:** rotate first, clean up second.

## How a secret ends up in a settings file

Developer machines hold secrets: a database connection string in a config file, cloud keys in local installations, an API token in .env. Ask Claude Code to check why login fails on staging or to run a migration, and the command it proposes carries that secret, because it can’t work without it. Claude Code asks before it runs a shell command, multiple times a session. Pick "Yes, and don't ask again" and it runs the command and adds a permission rule to `.claude/settings.local.json` in the project folder, so it won't ask again. The rule is the command string itself:

This is Claude Code's own behavior, not the model's: it happens with Anthropic's latest models too, and we reproduced it with Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

The file is meant to stay on the developer’s machine, and Claude Code tries to keep it there. When it creates the file inside a git repo, it adds it to the developer's _global_ git ignore list. That covers the common case. It doesn’t cover a folder that becomes a repo later, a clone on another machine, or a file someone already committed. The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it.

Often Claude commits the file itself. In 539 of the 1,105 repos with a real secret that we traced, a commit co-authored by Claude changed the file. Those commits name every recent model, from Sonnet 4.5 to Opus 5.5.

## Who is exposed

63 organizations hold a real secret in a public allowlist. The strongest cases, all in `.claude/settings.local.json` and each checked at a pinned commit:

| Organization | What’s exposed |
| --- | --- |
| Database vendor | Its own cloud API key with manage access and no expiry claim, plus the cluster host |
| B2B startup | Production Azure Postgres password |
| Software agency | Square production access token |
| Open-source project (over 1,000 stars) | OpenAI-format API key |
| Open-source project | npm token |
| IT services firm (medical-records app) | Owner password for the app’s cloud Postgres database |
| Payments startup | Postgres password for the postgres role |

Most are companies: startups, software agencies, IT services firms. A few are established vendors, exposed through their own demo and workshop repos. Nobody meant to publish a key. The key was in a command, the command was approved, and the file was committed with everything else.

The allowlists also hold server logins: 43 SSH credentials for public servers, some of them a root password in an `sshpass` command. One university repo, for example, permanently approved a root SSH command to a public server.

## How many

Public GitHub holds 104,185 copies of .claude/settings.local.json, in 103,617 repositories. 1,122 files (1.1%) hold a real secret: a key in a known provider format, or a password or token next to a public host. Together they hold 1,379 distinct secrets: 636 provider keys and 743 passwords or tokens for public hosts.

More than a third open a database directly: 379 database passwords and 122 Supabase service-role keys. Another 103 are Supabase account tokens, which control every project in the account. The rest are mostly API tokens for third-party services and AI model keys, plus 43 SSH logins, 42 GitHub, GitLab and npm tokens, 23 AWS keys and 6 private keys.

Large allowlists drive the rate. One in ten files over 8 KB holds a real secret, against fewer than one in 500 under 500 bytes. The longer a developer has been clicking “don’t ask again”, the more the file holds.

The files are still there: every one sat on its repo’s default branch on November 2, 2026, and most have sat there a long time. In the median repo with a real secret, the file was first committed 217 days before that. In 118 repos, more than a year before.
 Forks copy them: 211 forks of 74 repos carry the same secrets.

Deleting the file doesn’t solve it. Earlier versions of the file hold 734 real secrets, in 509 repos, that appear in no current copy, usually because the file was deleted.

Counting the file's history, the shared settings file and agent transcripts (next sections), the total comes to 2,539 distinct real secrets in 1,994 repos.

## What secret scanners miss

Generic secret scanners miss many of these. We ran **gitleaks** and **TruffleHog** over all 104,185 files. Of the 1,122 files with a real secret, gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643; 215 were flagged by neither.

The gap is passwords inside commands. Scanners look for key formats: a provider prefix, a long random string. A password typed after `PGPASSWORD=`, `sshpass -p` or `mysql -p`, or a bearer header in a curl call, is an ordinary word in an ordinary command line, and both tools mostly let it through.

This matters beyond this file. The same password-in-a-command pattern appears wherever an agent records what it ran: transcripts, memory files, handoff notes, and a scanner tuned to key formats misses it in all of them.

## Not just one file

The allowlist is the clearest case, but agents write secrets into other files developers commit.

| File | Checked | With a real secret |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared .claude/settings.json | All 76,011 | 298 files |
| Agent chat transcripts (.specstory, aider, Cursor exports) | 2,523 | 120 files in 87 repos |
| Agent memory files (MEMORY.md and similar) | 1,200 | 9 repos |
| Handoff and deploy notes | 2,095 | 33 files |
| VS Code Copilot auto-approve settings | 173 | 9 repos |

Teams commit the shared settings file on purpose, and most of its secrets sit in allow rules as exact command lines. A third of the handoff notes with a secret were written by the agent itself.

The file leaks beyond GitHub too. Of 31,053 Hugging Face Spaces, 126 hold .claude/settings.local.json, and one has allow rules with a database service key and a user password. On GitLab.com, 2 of the 69 public copies we checked hold a real secret, including a GitLab access token.

The habit that leaks is the same everywhere: typing a secret into a command that an agent then records.

## On the developer's machine

Most of these files never reach GitHub. They stay on developers’ machines, and that doesn’t make them safe. The allowlist is plain JSON in the project folder.

Malware already collects credentials from developer machines in bulk. In September 2025 the [Shai-Hulud npm worm](https://sysdig.com/blog/shai-hulud-the-novel-self-replicating-worm-infecting-hundreds-of-npm-packages) downloaded TruffleHog and ran it over the victim’s files. That scanner flags 643 of the 1,122 files with a real secret. Three weeks earlier, the [malicious Nx packages](https://blog.gitguardian.com/the-nx-s1ngularity-attack-inside-the-credential-leak/) told the developer’s own Claude Code and Gemini CLI to search the disk for secrets.

The file can also leave without git: in a published npm package, a Docker image built with a copy command, a zip archive or a synced folder. And a secret approved once stays in the file until someone deletes the rule, long after the command ran.

## Prior work

This post adds the full GitHub count of secrets leakage at scale, the organization cases, the scanner gap, and the other agent files that carry the same secrets. Claude Code users have reported the mechanism in GitHub issues since August 2025 ([#5544](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/5544), [#11982](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/11982), [#13106](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/13106), [#91270](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/91270)). None got a reply from Anthropic, and three were closed automatically as inactive or duplicate. ironPeak found the same file in their own repo in February 2026 and measured 2.4% of repos with AI config folders carrying secrets in history, on a sample of 100. Lakera found credentials in 33 such files across 30 npm packages in April.

## What to do

**Developers:**

1.   If the file is tracked in a repo, untrack it with git rm --cached `.claude/settings.local.json` and add it to the repo’s own .gitignore.
2.   Rotate every credential the file has ever held. Removing it doesn’t clear git history, forks or clones.
3.   Even if the file was never committed, open it and delete every rule that contains a secret.
4.   Stop typing secrets into commands. Reference them as $VAR from whatever secrets manager you use, so the rule records $DB_URL, not the secret.
5.   Approve patterns, like `Bash(npm run:*)`, instead of literal commands.

**Security teams:**

1.   Treat agent folders: .claude/, .cursor/, .gemini/, .specstory/, agent memory files, as secret-bearing, like .env, on laptops as well as in repos.
2.   Add them to pre-commit and CI secret scanning, including history. Make sure the scanner catches passwords inside commands (PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p, mysql -p, bearer headers), not only provider key formats.
3.   Add .claude/settings.local.json to your org’s .gitignore templates.
4.   Triage credentials paired with public hosts first: those are the ones that give access.

## Disclosure

We reported each organization case to its owner on November 2 and 3, 2026. One company confirmed its key had been live.

## Method and limits

**Collection.** All data came from read-only GitHub code and commit search on default branches, November 1 to 3, 2026. Code search returns at most 1,000 results per query, so we split the search by file size until every slice fit under the cap.
