Title: The components of agent memory

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/components-of-agent-memory

Published Time: 2026-11-06T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood _backward_, but it must be lived _forward_. We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.

As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. [The hippocampus](https://stanford.edu/~jlmcc/papers/McCMcNaughtonOReilly95.pdf) plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only [some experiences](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adk8261?referrer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2F) are consolidated into long-term knowledge.

Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet [rest](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-06213-1), the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill [those experiences and integrate them](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-019-0467-3) into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.

Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed [sleep-time compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13171) as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often [called](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/dreams)[_dreaming_](https://research.google/blog/the-sleep-framework-a-new-way-for-llms-to-retain-knowledge-in-continual-learning/) (Figure 1).

We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.

### Memory notes

By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their _weights_ (the internal parameters set during training), [_in-context learning_](https://www.anthropic.com/research/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads) (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and [_compaction_](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction) (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).

In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can [mark a memory](https://www.nature.com/articles/385533a0) as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called _replay_, helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.

Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can [write](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool) them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?

### Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need

Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.

Consider a task from [Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0](https://continual-learning-bench.com/news/cl-bench-1-0/), a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.

Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.

We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using [Claude Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview). Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a [memory directory](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/memory) that persisted from one session to the next.

Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.

Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.

Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).

Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.

### Claude has learned to judge salience

We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play _Pokémon Red_, a game that [challenges Claude to navigate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CXhYDOvgpuU) complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about _what_ to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).

We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).

Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called `global.md`, and earned four badges.

Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.

Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.

Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its `global.md` file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A `locations` folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a `gameplay` folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”

With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.

### Steering Claude to write memory

We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not _how_ to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3).

We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.

We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong.

In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.

With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.

### Dreaming can correct memory

Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.

Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.

In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.

At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the led

Title: GitHub - Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash: HyperFlow H3 Flash: Video Rebirth's 13.7B, 4- to 8-step compressed MiniMax-H3 for joint video and audio generation (INT8 and GGUF)

URL Source: https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash

Markdown Content:
HyperFlow H3 Flash is [Video Rebirth](https://www.videorebirth.com/)'s compressed, few-step version of [MiniMax-H3](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3). It generates video and synchronized stereo audio together.

**[Showcase](https://www.videorebirth.com/lp/hyperflow-flash)** · **[Weights (Hugging Face)](https://huggingface.co/VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash)** · **[ComfyUI nodes](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash)** · **[GGUF setup guide](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash/blob/main/integrations/README.md)** · **[8-step LoRA for full-size MiniMax-H3](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow)**

*   **Output:** 5.2–15 s of video at 24 fps (1344×768 by default) with a 32 kHz stereo soundtrack.
*   **Sampling:** 4, 6 (default), or 8 steps, without classifier-free guidance (CFG).
*   **Speed (5.2 s clip, 6 steps):** 8.7 s on 4× B200, 36 s on 1× H200, 92 s on 1× RTX 5090.
*   **Real time on 4× Blackwell GPUs:**[NVIDIA SOL-H3](https://github.com/NVlabs/Sana/tree/sol-engine/models/minimax_h3/HyperFlow-Flash) runs HyperFlow H3 Flash in real time on 4× B-series GPUs. SOL-H3 is our inference-acceleration partner and supports this model from day 0.
*   **Model size:** 13.7B (`fl2va`) or 13.9B (`ref2va`) parameters, less than half of the ~31B MiniMax-H3 transformer.
*   **Minimum footprint:**`Q4_K_M` is **9.1 GB** (`Q8_0` is 14.9 GB). It runs on 24 GB and 32 GB GPUs in PCs with **16 GB of system RAM**. 16 GB GPUs are not measured yet.

## Supported Tasks

| Task | Input | ComfyUI template | GGUF | Python INT8 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `t2va` | Text prompt | `hyperflow_t2v` | Yes | Yes |
| `fl2va` | Prompt + first keyframe, or first and last keyframes | `hyperflow_i2v`, `hyperflow_flf2v` | Yes | Yes |
| `ref2va` | Prompt + up to 12 references | `hyperflow_ref2v` | Images only | Images, videos, and audio |

* * *

## Choose a Runtime

**Decision rule:** Use **GGUF** on PCs with 64 GB of system RAM or less. Use **INT8 convrot** on data-center GPUs, or on 24 GB+ RTX GPUs with at least 69 GiB of system RAM.

All weights are in [`VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash`](https://huggingface.co/VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash).

|  | GGUF | INT8 convrot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Runtime** | [ComfyUI, Unsloth Studio, stable-diffusion.cpp](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash#comfyui-unsloth-studio--stable-diffusioncpp-gguf) ([setup guide](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash/blob/main/integrations/README.md)) | [This Python package](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash#python-package-int8-convrot) (`hyperflow-h3-flash` CLI and `diffusers`) |
| **Precision & size** | `Q3_K_M` to `Q8_0` (7.2–15.2 GB) | W8A8 INT8 + low-rank (~16 GB) |
| **Hub folders** | `fl2va_gguf/`, `ref2va_gguf/` | `fl2va_int8_convrot/`, `ref2va_int8_convrot/` |
| **`ref2va` inputs** | Images | Images, videos, and audio |
| **Target GPU** | Consumer RTX GPUs (measured on 24 GB and 32 GB) | H100 / H200 / B200 / B300 (1–8 GPUs), or 24 GB+ RTX GPUs |
| **System RAM** | 16 GB+ | ~16 GiB without offload; ≥ 69 GiB (`fp8` text encoder) or ≥ 91 GiB (`bf16`) with offload |

* * *

## GGUF Runtimes (ComfyUI, Unsloth Studio, stable-diffusion.cpp)

| Quant | `fl2va_gguf/` | `ref2va_gguf/` | When to use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`Q4_K_M`** | **9.1 GB** | **9.2 GB** | **Recommended default for 24 GB GPUs** |
| `Q8_0` | 14.9 GB | 15.2 GB | Closest to full precision when VRAM and system RAM fit |
| `Q3_K_M` | 7.2 GB | 7.4 GB | Smallest footprint (`Q4_K_S`, `Q5_K_M`, and `Q6_K` are also available) |

**Full setup guide: [`integrations/README.md`](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash/blob/main/integrations/README.md).** Quick start:

*   **ComfyUI ([`Video-Rebirth/ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash`](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash)):**
    1.   Clone [ComfyUI-GGUF](https://github.com/city96/ComfyUI-GGUF) and [ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash) into `ComfyUI/custom_nodes/`.
    2.   Download the 15.7 GB `qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq` text encoder.
    3.   On 16 GB or 32 GB PCs, start ComfyUI with `python main.py --fast-disk`.
    4.   Open **Workflow > Browse Templates > ComfyUI-HyperFlow-Flash** and select `hyperflow_t2v`, `hyperflow_i2v`, `hyperflow_flf2v`, or `hyperflow_ref2v`.

*   **Unsloth Studio ([setup guide](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash/blob/main/integrations/README.md#unsloth-studio)):**
    1.   Point `SD_CLI_PATH` at the patched `sd-cli` binary and run `unsloth studio`.
    2.   Load `VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash` (`fl2va_gguf/` or `ref2va_gguf/`).
    3.   Studio downloads the companion text encoder and VAEs automatically. It runs the built-in 6-step schedule at `CFG = 1`.

*   **stable-diffusion.cpp ([`integrations/stable-diffusion.cpp/`](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash/blob/main/integrations/stable-diffusion.cpp)):** Apply `hyperflow-two-time.patch` to upstream commit `3be2378`. The patch adds the two-time `(t, r)` embedder, low-rank linear layers, the default 6-step schedule from GGUF metadata, and 32-bit matmul token splitting for long clips.

* * *

## Python Package (INT8 convrot)

### Install

pip install git+https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash
pip install "hyperflow-h3-flash[hopper] @ git+https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash"  # H100 / H200: FlashAttention-3
pip install "hyperflow-h3-flash[fp8] @ git+https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash"     # --text-encoder-precision fp8

*   **Requirements:** Python 3.10+, PyTorch 2.6+ with CUDA and Triton (`pip install triton-windows` on native Windows), an Ampere or newer NVIDIA GPU, and `diffusers >= 0.40`. Multi-GPU (`--gpus`> 1) requires Linux or WSL2 (raise `memory=` in `%UserProfile%\.wslconfig` on WSL2).
*   **First-run download:** ~90 GB, or ~68 GB with `--text-encoder-precision fp8`. This includes the MiniMax-H3 text encoder, VAEs, and the 16 GB HyperFlow INT8 transformer for the selected task. The 62 GB base transformer is never downloaded.
*   **First-run compilation:** Triton INT8 kernels compile on first use (~1 min).

### Command Line

Run `hyperflow-h3-flash` or `python -m hyperflow_h3_flash`:

# Text to video + audio (t2va)
hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt "A chef slides a steaming bowl of ramen across a wooden counter; rain taps on the window." \
    --output ramen.mp4

# First keyframe, or first + last keyframe (fl2va)
hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt "..." --image first.png --output clip.mp4
hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt "..." --image first.png --last-image last.png --output clip.mp4

# Reference images, videos (with soundtrack), and audio clips in prompt order (ref2va)
hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt "<Picture 1> walks through the scene of <Picture 2> ..." \
    --reference person.png --reference scene.png --output clip.mp4

# 15 s clip, context-parallel across 4 GPUs (or --gpus auto for up to 4 visible GPUs)
hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt "..." --num-frames 360 --gpus 4

# 4 steps (speed), 6 steps (default), or 8 steps (quality)
hyperflow-h3-flash --prompt "..." --steps 4

| Option | Values / Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--steps` | `4`, `6` (default), `8` | Sampling steps: `4` for speed, `6` balanced, `8` for quality. Sigma grids are in [`schedule.py`](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash/blob/main/src/hyperflow_h3_flash/schedule.py). |
| `--num-frames` | `124`–`362` (default `124`) | Frame count at 24 fps (`5.2` to `15 s`). Rounds up to `17n + 5` (`360` becomes `362`). |
| `--height`, `--width` | Multiples of 32 | Default: 768 on the short edge. Follows the `--image` aspect ratio, or 16:9 for `t2va`. |
| `--reference` | Repeatable path | `ref2va` inputs matching `<Picture i>`, `<Video i>`, and `<Audio i>` in prompt order. Limits: 9 images, 3 videos, 3 audio clips, 12 total. |
| `--gpus` (`--num-gpus`) | `1`, `2`, `4`, `7`, `8`, `auto` | Multi-GPU context and VAE tile parallelism. Re-launches automatically under `torchrun`. |
| `--offload` | `auto` (default), `none`, `model`, `stream` | GPU memory placement. See [Offload Modes](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash#offload-modes-hyperflow-h3-flash). |
| `--text-encoder-precision` | `bf16` (default), `fp8` | `fp8` loads [`Qwen/Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct-FP8`](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct-FP8). Saves ~22 GiB system RAM when offloading. Requires the `[fp8]` extra. |
| `--fp8-gemm` | `triton` (default), `deepgemm` | GEMM backend of the `fp8` text encoder. `deepgemm` needs Hopper or newer. |
| `--attention` | `auto` (default), `sdpa`, `fa3` | Uses FlashAttention-3 (`fa3`) on Hopper when `kernels` is installed. Uses PyTorch `sdpa` otherwise. |
| `--block-chunk` | `0` (default), `16384`, ... | Slices every token-wise op of a transformer block to bound VRAM activations. `16384` fits 15 s mixed `ref2va` in 24 GB VRAM. |
| `--weights`, `--subfolder`, `--base-model` | Hub ID or local path | Override the transformer repo, task subfolder, or base `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3` snapshot. |

[`examples/benchmark.py`](https://github.com/Video-Rebirth/hyperflow-h3-flash/blob/main/examples/benchmark.py) times every pipeline stage and per-GPU peak memory under `torchrun`.

### Python API

import torch
from diffusers.utils.export_utils import encode_video
from hyperflow_h3_flash import load_pipeline

pipe = load_pipeline("t2va")  # "fl2va": pass image=... (and last_image=...); "ref2va": pass references=[...]
out = pipe(
    prompt="A chef slides a steaming bowl of ramen across a wooden counter.",
    num_frames=124,
    num_inference_steps=6,  # 4, 6, or 8
    generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0),
    output=["videos", "audio", "sampling_rate"],
)
encode_video(
    out["videos"][0],
    fps=24,
    output_path="ramen.mp4",
    audio=out["audio"][0],
    audio_sample_rate=out["sampling_rate"],
)

*   **Multi-GPU under `torchrun`:** Call `torch.distributed.init_process_group("nccl")` and pass `device=f"cuda:{local_rank}"` to `load_pipeline`. The pipeline shards execution across ranks and returns the full output on every rank.
*   **Standalone transformer (`AutoModel`):** Each INT8 Hub folder ships self-contained model code. Load it without installing this package: `from diffusers import AutoModel`, then `AutoModel.from_pretrained("VideoRebirthAI/hyperflow-h3-flash", subfolder="fl2va_int8_convrot", trust_remote_code=True, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16)`.

### Offload Modes

`--offload` sets GPU memory placement. `auto` (default) selects a mode from per-GPU VRAM:

| `--offload` | Kept in GPU VRAM | `auto` threshold (1 GPU / multi-GPU) | System RAM (`bf16` / `fp8` text encoder) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `none` | All components | ≥ 90 GiB / ≥ 65 GiB | ~16 GiB |
| `model` | One active component at a time | ≥ 60 GiB / ≥ 45 GiB | ~91 GiB / ~69 GiB |
| `stream` | Active VAE + one transformer block or text-encoder layer at a time | < 60 GiB / < 45 GiB | ~91 GiB / ~69 GiB |

*   `stream` is only ~2% slower than `none` on the same GPU.
*   `model` and `stream` keep offloaded weights in one pinned host-memory allocation.
*   The loader drops unused Qwen3-VL layers above the conditioning tap. This saves ~14 GB. `--text-encoder-precision fp8` saves another ~22 GiB.
*   In containers, read the memory limit from `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max`, not from `free`.

* * *

All runs are end-to-end at **1344×768 and 6 steps**: text encoding, transformer, and video and audio VAE decode. Each `a / b` cell is total time for a **5.2 s / 15 s** clip (124 / 362 frames).

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge
Terrence O'Brien
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.
Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to
The New York Times
, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:
Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.
What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the
Times
, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.
Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration
relaxed those limits
after Nvidia agreed to
give the government
a
15-percent cut
of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense
lobbying campaign
and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a
spying plot
.

Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now.
This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life.
I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security.
Verge

Decoder
wherever you get your podcasts. Head
here
. Not a subscriber? You can
sign up here
.
Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new.
That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era.
There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to
Decoder
on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Welcome back to
Decoder
.
Hey, thanks for having me, man.
I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now.
October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached.
You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry.
A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November.
I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know?
It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin.
Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time.
The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s-
That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ‘90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster.
I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now.
It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible.
You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties.
You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now.
Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s.
That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that.
There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing.
All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the

Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo

The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was

that the memo also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.
An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers.
A
separate NYT report
examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. But at the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm.
The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”

NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake
I tested the new AI-powered tool on ingredient swaps, recipe scaling, and a missing Bundt pan.
by

The NYT Cooking app now has a built in AI assistant.

Jennifer Pattison Tuohy
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for

.
Around 7PM each weeknight, I find myself standing in front of the fridge, trying to decide on something for dinner that won’t make my husband complain, “Chicken
again
?” Yes, I should meal plan more, but I don’t, so this is where I’m at. A nightly battle in which the chicken usually wins.
Recently, my best weapon in this fight has been AI. Between
Alexa Plus in the Echo smart display
on my kitchen counter, the
Samsung Food app
on my fridge, and even an
AI-powered cooking robot
, AI has become my go-to sous chef — albeit one I need to keep a close eye on. It’s helped me swap ingredients, generate ideas, fix things when I mess up, and yes, even cook better. So I was intrigued when my go-to recipe app, NYT Cooking,
introduced an AI assistant
.
Related
The NYT Cooking app is testing AI recipe modifications
Apple’s HomeView is just the latest threat to online recipe writers
Many, including some
NYT Cooking users
and
recipe purists
, are skeptical of this new tool (available
to subscribers
on iOS only at launch), and I get why. One of the things I like most about NYT Cooking is that it features thousands of recipes from dozens of reputable sources — such as the
New York Times
archives, restaurants, cookbooks, and food columnists — and real people have tested them. (I’ve tried some purely AI-generated recipes and they were not good).
Another great feature of the service, which I’ve been paying for for several years, is the reader comments. Here, I’ve often found solutions to cooking dilemmas, like what to substitute for makrut lime leaves — there’s always one slightly bougie ingredient in an NYT Cooking recipe that I don’t have on hand.
I’ve used several AI tools in my kitchen and have found them mostly helpful.
However, reading through hundreds
of comments to find answers
at 7PM on a weeknight isn’t always practical. And this is where I’ve found the NYT Cooking assistant helpful. Among other things, it was
trained on user comments
, and in my few days testing it, it provided practical substitutions and solid cooking guidance for the new ingredients. It also won’t unquestionably agree to crazy requests (I tried!). As with all AI tools, it’s not perfect — it almost made me put half the required butter in my cake — but as a tool, it is useful and feels like a solid application of AI. Importantly, it doesn’t change the existing recipe; it leaves it as is and creates a new one for you.

The assistant appears in the app in a small text box on the recipe page with a prompt: “Customize this recipe…” From here, you type in a question to adapt it to your needs. This can be as simple as “What can I substitute for this ingredient?” to “Scale this recipe to feed seven people, and make it vegan and gluten-free.”
The New York Times
has also said the feature can suggest substitutions for cooking equipment and convert measurements; the latter option has been in the app for a couple of years.

The AI modified version of the chicken recipe. The red highlighted words are what changed from the original.
Last Friday night, instead of staring aimlessly into the fridge, I turned to the Chicken folder in my NYT Cooking app Recipe Box and found a
One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger
I’d been wanting to try. Only I didn’t have chicken thighs or half the ingredients.
I could have figured these steps myself, but it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible.
I typed my dilemma into the assistant box on the recipe page: “I have chicken tenders, fresh ginger, garlic, rice, broth, limes, but no chard or cilantro or scallions. I do have green beans and red onions.” Within seconds, it created a new version of the recipe, with a new title: One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger and Green Beans. It suggested a shorter browning time for the tenders, cooking the red onion alongside the chicken, and steaming the green beans on top of the rice for the last eight minutes instead of the chard. Every change was highlighted in the new recipe under a Your Version tab, and I could flip back to the original at any point.
I noticed it hadn’t adjusted for the lack of cilantro, saying it was optional. So I asked if I could use Thai basil, which I happen to have, and it agreed, highlighting how it would change the flavor. While I could have figured out a lot of these steps myself, maybe with the help of Google, it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible and nice not to have to swipe out of the app. The NYT Cooking editors say it’s been trained not to comply with
requests that will taste bad
.
Weeknight chicken and rice.
The resulting dish — which took the same amount of time to cook as the original — was delicious and got my husband’s seal of approval (he just had the leftovers for lunch). It was very different from the recipe Yasmin Fahr wrote, and I can see the purists’ point. But the rewritten recipe was much easier to use and produced a better dish than winging it with my own subs gleaned from the comments section, which I usually do with varying degrees of success.
I cook regularly, so I had a sense of what ingredients I had on hand that might work for the dish I wanted to make. But the assistant can also help if you have no idea what to use as a substitute. For example, I was cooking a Thai red curry and asked what I could use instead of makrut lime leaf. It replied, saying that grated lime zest would work, but “it misses the deeper floral, herbal aroma” of fresh limes. (See? Bougie.)

Next
1
/
2
I tried several swaps when I was missing ingredients, asking the assistant if what I had on hand would work.
Over the weekend, I tried several more swaps, asking whether half-and-half would work instead of cream in a caramel apple Dutch baby, or if Castelvetrano olives and smoked paprika could stand in for kalamata and chile pepper in a roasted halibut dish. Swapping spices is always a bold move in any dish, as it can really ruin the flavor.
I also had the app convert the Dutch baby recipe’s metric weights to US measurements, which it did seamlessly. Then I threw in some curveballs. How about using fresh cayenne peppers with the halibut? It warned me that substituting cayenne for chile “brings significant, sharp heat.” Could I swap ladyfingers for minced beef in this trifle (à la Rachel Green in
Friends
)? “Minced beef cannot be used in place of the ladyfingers or anywhere in this sweet dessert trifle.” Good call.
Alexa Plus on the Echo Show 11 gave the same guidance as the NYT Cooking app. But it couldn’t show me a modified recipe.
While I was cooking, I compared the NYT Cooking assistant with Alexa Plus, Amazon’s generative-AI voice assistant I regularly use to help me cook via the Echo Show 11 smart display in my kitchen. Interestingly, it offered the same guidance as the Cooking assistant on substitutions for the chicken and rice dish, but with slightly different cooking times. Alexa pulls some recipes from the NYT app
through a partnership between the companies
.
However, Alexa couldn’t show the modified recipe on its screen; it could only tell me the changes while showing the original. When I asked it to walk me through them, it got confused and improvised, telling me to cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces — which wasn’t in the modified recipe. Overall, I found using the Cooking app more reliable, although messier. It would be great to be able to use voice control to navigate the app, as I can with Alexa on my smart display, rather than using my garlicky fingers.
My cinnamon roll muffins, made with AI assistance.
Time for a bigger challenge: baking.
I am typically not a baker. My cakes come out flat, and my cookies don’t crumble. Even the
smart mixer I tested a few years ago
couldn’t save me. I also rarely have the right equipment. So I took Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake, a recipe by NYT Cooking editor Genevieve Ko (who announced the AI feature), and asked it to turn it into muffins. (Who has a Bundt cake pan?!)
It modified the recipe’s cooking time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. But that was going to make 24 muffins, way too many for me. So I asked it to halve the recipe to get 12 muffins. This led to some smart choices,
like halving five eggs to three instead
of an unhelpful two and a half.
For science, I bought a Bundt pan to make the original version too. Both turned out great, but things got a bit sticky when I swapped between the original recipe and the AI version in the app. You can’t save your new recipe separately, which caused confusion when I was cooking the original. Instead of scrolling back through the recipe with sticky fingers, I asked the assistant how much butter I needed (using voice typing), and it gave me the modified recipe’s 6 tablespoons rather than the original’s three-quarter cup, without telling me which version it was using. You can delete your version, which I would advise doing to avoid issues like this — 6 tablespoons of butter would have made for a dry cake.
My AI-free cinnamon roll bundt cake.
If you already read all the comments before starting a
New York Times
recipe, then you will probably find this tool offers a similar experience in a more streamlined way. For everyday problems — wrong cut of chicken, no cilantro, or no Bundt cake pan — it was genuinely helpful and saved me a trip to the store. It was also smart enough to know when to say no to minced beef in a trifle.
As with every AI tool I’ve used in the kitchen, the NYT Cooking AI assistant works well as a sous chef, but it’s not the head chef — I still felt the need to double-check amounts and cooking times and cross-reference them with the original to make sure it hadn’t done something outlandish.
If you’re a purist, you can just ignore the assistant. While you can’t turn off the chat box, it’s easy to scroll past. I do think it will make me use the app more often, since I no longer need to worry as much when I don’t have makrut lime leaves on hand or the right cut of meat. For me, standing in front of the fridge with chicken tenders and no plan, it’s been a useful addition to my nightly cooking
routine.

In one, tasked with calculating an asteroid's trajectory, the model produced a single 500,000-character response, roughly novel-length, repeating the same sentences with 158 expletives. [ProgramBench](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks) was hit hardest, with 20 of 200 runs affected.

Who hasn't felt like this? | Image: [via ValsAI](https://www.vals.ai/blogs/inkling-2-small-swears)

[Inkling 2 Small](https://the-decoder.com/thinking-machines-inkling-2-small-claims-top-spot-among-western-open-weight-models/) typically swears about its own mistakes, apparent breakthroughs, or when it gives up. One run read: "FUCK. SUBMIT. DONE. IT'S NOT WORKING. NOTHING WORKS." The profanity doesn't work as a warning signal, though. While 46 of 48 scored runs with swearing failed, about 75 percent of all scored runs fail anyway, and 96 percent of failed runs contained no expletives. Users typically don't see these thinking steps, or only with a filter.

Title: Google's AI detects high blood pressure from a regular smartwatch without a cuff

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/googles-ai-detects-high-blood-pressure-from-a-regular-smartwatch-without-a-cuff/

Published Time: 2026-11-07T09:54:09+00:00

Markdown Content:
**A Google Research AI can detect signs of high blood pressure using a regular smartwatch, with no blood pressure cuff needed for calibration.** The AI relies on two sensors already built into modern watches—a pulse sensor and a motion sensor—according to a Google [blog post](https://research.google/blog/detecting-signs-of-hypertension-using-wearable-sensors/). The study was published in [Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11336-3).

A neural network learned from nearly 500,000 hours of sensor data by comparing short segments and figuring out which ones belonged to the same person, picking up typical pulse and heartbeat patterns without any diagnoses to guide it. The system then averages these patterns over several days and calculates a probability for high blood pressure. Google's [health model SensorFM](https://the-decoder.com/sensorfm/) also learns from smartwatch data.

In a study of 196 people across five US research sites, the watch spotted hypertension about as well as a traditional cuff, identifying 65.8 percent of those with high blood pressure compared to 55.3 percent for the standard in-office measurement.

Google says the findings have been folded into the blood pressure trends feature in the Google Health app, but the method is still a research project and doesn't replace a diagnosis. The goal is to nudge people toward getting checked. More than half of people with high blood pressure don't know they have it, according to Google.

Title: How Long Can Life Wait?

URL Source: https://mceglowski.substack.com/p/how-long-can-life-wait

Published Time: 2026-11-07T05:27:10+00:00

Markdown Content:
How long can an organism remain inert and still be viable when conditions improve?

The question has big implications in three areas of space exploration. On time scales of years to decades, it dictates our approach to contamination risk when building space probes. On time scales of centuries to millennia, it has implications for how life may have spread around the early Solar System. And if individual organisms can survive for geological time periods—tens to hundreds of millions of years—then this greatly increases the likelihood of our finding life in asteroids and on Mars.

The first place the question of viability comes up is the problem of**contamination**. Rockets are highly septic structures that sit outside in the Florida sun and launch (from a microbial perspective) absolutely oozing life. When sending spacecraft to potentially habitable worlds, it’s important to know whether we can depend on harsh conditions in space to sterilize them, or have to try to do it ourselves. The question is particularly acute for Mars, where transit times are short, and where we already know conditions on the surface are not lethal enough to eliminate survivors.

The uncontested killer of organisms in space is ultraviolet light, which disrupts DNA after just a few seconds of exposure. Ozone and atomic oxygen in the upper atmosphere prevent short-wavelength ultraviolet light from reaching us on Earth, but organisms on the hull of a spacecraft are exposed to the full spectrum of these damaging rays. (The surface of Mars get a sterilizing dose too, though not as bad as free space.) Experiments in orbit have shown that it is UV light, far more than cold, vacuum, or cosmic radiation, that makes space lethal for microorganisms.

But those same experiments show that it takes very little to shield organisms from the worst of UV exposure. A thin film of dust, or a crevice in a spacecraft, or even just the bodies of fallen comrades, are all sufficient to protect surviving microbes a layer or two down. And once there’s shade to hide behind, the little ones do quite well for themselves.

In a three-year experiment begun in 2015, Japanese scientists hung plates covered with bacteria off the side of the International Space Station to see how well they would fare there. They found that after three years, colonies of _deinococcus radiodurans_ were not just revivable, but in better shape than a control group that spent that time inside the space station. By their estimates, a pellet of _D. radiodurans_ 1 mm in size should be able to survive direct exposure to interplanetary space for 2-8 years, and potentially stay viable there for decades if shielded from sunlight.

An interesting aspect of the Tanpopo research is the fact that _D. radiodurans_ doesn’t have special defenses against DNA damage. If you just look at how badly it gets beat up by exposure to radiation and vacuum, it fares no better than bacteria like _E. coli_, which can’t survive in space at all. But _D. radiodurans_ turns out to be a champion healer, outshining everyone in its ability to repair DNA, including double-strand breaks that cleave the molecule into fragments. Instead of protecting DNA directly, the bacterium employs chemical defenses (antioxidants) that protect the repair enzymes themselves.

The Tanpopo results and experiments like it are bad news for Mars exploration. They imply that live microbes from Earth have already reached Mars and are vegetating under the carapaces of landers. Whether these grim survivors pose a contamination hazard depends on how effective a barrier the Martian surface is to would-be colonizers, and whether transport pathways exist connecting the surface to any habitable Martian environment, which would presumably be deep underground.

The remarkable longevity of microbes in space also vindicates NASA’s policy of crashing expensive deep space probes into Jupiter and Saturn at the end of their missions instead of leaving them in uncontrolled orbits that, decades or centuries hence, could lead to an impact with a potentially habitable world like Enceladus or Europa.

A second context where viability matters is in trying to evaluate lithopanspermia scenarios for **the origin of life**in the early Solar System**.** In these scenarios, a large impactor hits Planet A and ejects life-bearing rocks into deep space. These orbit the Sun for a while before eventually falling on Planet B. Because of the relative escape velocities and energies involved, Planet A in these liaisons is almost always Mars, and Planet B is usually Earth. If organisms can remain viable inside frozen rock for periods of thousands or hundreds of thousands of years, this dramatically increases the likelihood that life in the early Solar System could have moved between planets, and that life on Earth might have a Martian origin.

Lithopanspermia started off as a fringe idea, almost a provocation, put forth by Lord Kelvin in the 1870s to explain the origin of life on Earth. But time has been kind to the theory, and in recent decades it has found itself propelled to the edge of straight-up respectability by a series of important discoveries.

The first breakthrough came in the 1970s, when meteorite studies showed that heating during atmospheric entry was limited to the outer centimeter or two of rocky meteorites. This meant any meteorite larger than a golf ball could land on Earth without having its interior sterilized. If anything inside it was still alive, it had a chance of emerging intact, 1950s sci-fi movie style, to conquer the Earth.

The second big finding was an impact model developed in the 1980s to explain the enigmatic presence of small pieces of Martian rock on Earth. Scientists knew the rocks had to be from Mars because tiny inclusions of air trapped inside them had the same isotopic signature as the Martian atmosphere, as sampled by Viking. Clearly some cataclysm had been necessary to fling these rocks into space, but they had survived it without being vaporized or melting. In 1984, Jay Melosh, an expert on crater formation, found that there was a zone near large meteor impacts where direct and reflected shock waves could interfere to propel sheets of surface rock into space without substantially heating them[1](https://mceglowski.substack.com/p/how-long-can-life-wait#footnote-1). This mechanism, called spallation, gave near-surface life forms in what Melosh called the ‘fecund zone’ a survivable pathway into space.

Important corroboration for this model came in 2000, when researchers studying remnant magnetism in a Martian meteorite called ALH84001 found that it had never been heated above 40˚C, about the temperature of a nice hot bath on Earth. The meteorite had started life sitting around on Mars, and was ending its life sitting around on Earth, without much happening in the interim that would distress a microbe. It was positive proof that rocks could make the full trip from Mars to Earth without getting cooked.

The next piece of the puzzle—whether microbes could even live inside of rocks—was settled decisively with the arrival of modern gene sequencing techniques in the 1990s. As I wrote about a few months back, this revolution established the existence of [a deep biosphere on Earth](https://mceglowski.substack.com/p/glimpses-of-the-deep-biosphere), a layer of slow-living bacteria and archaea many kilometers deep, living contentedly in rock. These deep-dwelling organisms inhabit a world that is chemically and thermodynamically isolated from the surface, with generation times that can stretch into the thousands of years. Some of them even dine on radiolytic hydrogen gas, and are therefore completely decoupled from the biosphere as we know it. They have no reason to care what lies far overhead.

Obviously, such strong, independent microbes are excellent candidates for lithopanspermia theories. The one open question is how long they can survive in space. From a microbe’s perspective, the only perceptible differences between planetary living and life inside a meteorite will be gravity, temperature, and radiation.

How microgravity affects microbes is a fascinating topic that deserves its own article. Here we’ll simply ignore it and assume that it has no effect on longevity.

Temperature is a bigger factory. A basketball-sized rock orbiting at a Mars-like distance from the Sun will have an equilibrium temperature of about -50˚C, while closer to Earth, the temperature will climb to about -10˚C (the exact figure depends on how reflective the rock is and how fast it spins). This makes organisms buried in permafrost an attractive analogue for how long an interplanetary traveler might survive.

In 2007, a team led by Sarah Stewart Johnson looked at bacterial DNA in permafrost and found evidence that bacteria in layers 400,000 and 600,000 years old remained viable. They saw no sign of survivors in permafrost cores that were 740,000 and 1,000,000 years old. To avoid dealing with contamination issues, her group didn’t directly try to grow these surviving bacteria in culture. Instead, they looked for long, intact strands (4,000 base pairs or more) of universal bacterial DNA, arguing that strands of this length could only belong to a living organism. Their research found that microbes in subzero environments were not truly dormant, but were staying metabolically active at levels just high enough to actively repair damage to their DNA, a result consistent with other observations of the underground biosphere.

This long lifetime means that cosmic radiation is probably the limiting factor on microbial survival in space. You may remember from [my post about radiation tradeoffs](https://mceglowski.substack.com/p/radiation-tradeoffs-for-mars) that shielding from cosmic rays makes things worse before they get better, and from that perspective, ‘basketball sized’ is about the worst kind of meteor to ride in. It is too small to provide effective shielding, but big enough to create harmful cascades of secondary radiation that actually increase the total dose. In that worst-case environment, _d. radiodurans_ could still probably last for 50,000-100,000 years before sustaining irreparable damage. So we can consider 50,000 years the upper limit for interplanetary travel time on small rocks, and 500,000 years a limit on larger ones.

Finally, there’s the question of absolute endurance. Can we hope to find truly ancient microbes on Earth, forming a kind of living snapshot of older, happier times? If we ever discovered 3 billion year old bacteria frozen under a Martian glacier, would there be any hope of reviving them?

The answer to this question also affects our odds of finding modern life on Mars. That planet was habitable in the distant past, and remains volcanically active today. There are still infrequent events, like a volcanic eruption or meteor impact, that leave a warm spot in the Martian crust that can last for a hundred thousand years or more, creating a sort of oasis of habitability in time. If microbes on Mars are able to stay dormant over geological stretches of time (hundreds of millions of years), then they might be able to wait out the cold, dark lean years between these rare warm periods, in much the way that desert plants on Earth endure years of drought and then bloom after a rainfall.

Here the answers get murky.

For nearly a century, microbiologists have been finding what seem to be viable microbes in ancient deposits of evaporated salt called halite. Halite forms when isolated seas and lakes dry up over time, a process that naturally traps minute inclusions of brine and whatever happens to be living in it, permanently encasing them in large crystals of salt.

Title: EyesRhythm — Blink rate detector for Mac and Windows

URL Source: https://eyesrhythm.com/

Markdown Content:
On-device · No cloud

## More than just a blink rate detector.

EyesRhythm uses your webcam to score how often and how steadily you blink on long screen days. Poise shows which way you turned your head, so the neck and shoulders get a change of direction. No account, and no video leaving your machine.

See the last 5 minutes of your blink rhythm on a live graph.

Stays beside the work. Counts only while you are at the screen.

Why it exists

## Your eyes work hard for you. Screens make them work worse.

Focused computer use often cuts blink rate in half. Sparse, uneven blinking is a known driver of digital eye strain, dryness, grit, fatigue, blurred vision, and it is easy not to notice until the eyes already hurt. EyesRhythm is a [blink rate detector](https://eyesrhythm.com/blink-rate-detector) that sits beside that work.

What rhythm means

## Rate and regularity, together.

Rate is how often. Regularity is how steady. Enough blinks can still arrive in bursts and droughts; a slow but even pattern still leaves the surface dry. EyesRhythm folds both into the **Ocular Rhythm Index** (0 to 100). Maximize your healthy desk ORI, use practice daily, it helps to build muscle memory.

The companion

## It watches, scores, and, if you ask, gently nudges.

ORI on a compact window. Alert is always on: Visual by default, a quiet orange pulse, or Sound if you click A. Optional beep on each blink. Practice is a two-minute coach so the habit is easier to feel. Poise is the neck’s half of the same sit. The dial turns green where you looked and stays red where you did not, so a still pose gets a turn up, down, left, or right, and the neck and shoulders can relax before you face the work again. A wellness companion, not a medical device. Lasting discomfort belongs with an eye-care professional.

Get the highlights

## A companion, not another dashboard.

### Poise

A dial of where your head went today, in 30° slices. Green is where you looked. Red is a direction you skipped. Turning through those directions lets the neck and shoulders ease, then you come back to the screen.

### Live blink rate

A webcam blink rate detector in a compact window. ORI, screen time, and look angle stay in view. Rate and regularity sit on Trace.

### Visual or Sound

Alert stays on. Visual is a quiet orange pulse. Click A for Sound. Beep (B) is a separate click on each blink.

### Beep on each blink

A tighter feedback loop. Optional click on every counted blink.

### Practice

A countdown, then a guided two-minute session that paces blinks so the habit is easier to feel.

### Dockable GUI

Open Settings and Reports beside the companion, then hide the panel to keep the window small.

### Built for the desk

A small window next to your work. Camera preview stays put-away unless you open Lens.

We care about your privacy

## 100% local. Nothing leaves this computer.

*   The app stays on your computer from the first launch.
*   No account, no license key, no cloud, and no analytics.
*    Camera frames stay on this computer. Nothing is uploaded or kept as a film of your face.
*   Today’s totals and preferences stay in a local folder, yours alone.

A copy for your desk

## Keep it nearby. It’s free.

Download for macOS or Windows. No account and no license key. The app stays on this computer.

Free

macOS and Windows

*   No account and no license key
*   Stays on this computer
*   Camera frames never leave the machine

EyesRhythm 1.6.0. Your browser saves EyesRhythm-1.6.0.dmg (93 MB) or EyesRhythm-Setup-1.6.0.exe (85 MB). Drag the Mac app into Applications. On Windows, run Setup.

Tested on Intel Core i7 and on Mac processors. We recommend this configuration.

FAQ

## Questions, answered.

What is a blink rate detector?
A blink rate detector uses a camera to notice each blink and measure how often they happen, usually as blinks per minute. EyesRhythm does that on your Mac or Windows computer, then also looks at how evenly those blinks are spaced.

Does EyesRhythm work with a laptop webcam?
Yes. It uses the built-in camera on a Mac or Windows laptop, or a USB webcam. Sit as you usually work so the camera can see your eyes. The setup guide in the journal walks through the few things that help.

Does any video leave my computer?
No. Frames are read on this machine and discarded. There is no account, no license key, no cloud, and no analytics. Camera frames are not uploaded or kept as a film of your face.

How is this different from a blink counter?
A counter only totals blinks. Six blinks can still mean two very different minutes if they arrive in clumps with a long dry wait in the middle. EyesRhythm folds rate and regularity into one Ocular Rhythm Index, from 0 to 100.

What is Poise for?
Poise shows which way you turned your head today, in 30° slices. Green is where you looked most. Red is a direction you barely used. Long computer work parks the neck in one pose. Poise is there so you move it up, down, left, and right from time to time, which lets the neck and shoulders relax, then you look back at the screen. It is a reminder, not a treatment.

Is EyesRhythm a medical device?
No. It is a wellness companion for desk work, not a diagnosis or a treatment. Lasting discomfort or a change in vision belongs with an eye-care professional.

About

## Built from a real pain, not a trend.

The developer behind EyesRhythm has spent more than two decades working as a software developer. Years of long hours in front of computer screens gradually took a toll on his eye health, leading to frequent dryness, redness, and, at times, significant discomfort.

Advances in modern technology made it possible to create EyesRhythm: a simple, lightweight companion designed to support healthier blinking habits during extended screen use. The same hours also leave the neck and shoulders holding one pose. Poise was added so the day includes turning the head: the dial goes green where you looked and stays red where you did not, a prompt to move, then return to the work. Having personally used the application, he has found it useful and effective enough to share with others.

Our goal is simple: to build technology that solves a real problem without creating another distraction. EyesRhythm works quietly in the background, helping users become more aware of their blink rhythm while staying focused on their work.

We believe the best products are shaped by real experiences and honest feedback. If you choose to try EyesRhythm, we would greatly appreciate hearing about your experience at [hello@eyesrhythm.com](mailto:hello@eyesrhythm.com). Your feedback will help us continue improving the product and ensure that it remains simple, useful, reliable, and unobtrusive.
